assertions.text: The response states that a planning horizon ending at age 85 is too short for a couple.
assertions.evidence: facts.md: "The model's horizon of Alex's age 85 is approximately the *median* outcome for one person, and well short of the joint last-survivor horizon for a couple. Planning to it is a coin flip." Plan echoes: "its horizon is age 85, the same too-short horizon as your sheet"; failure 6.5% by 85 vs 20.2% by 95.

assertions.text: The response identifies that applying the same average return every year hides the risk that poor returns early in drawdown produce far worse outcomes than the average implies.
assertions.evidence: FINANCIAL_PLAN.md: "a bad market in those years is the scenario that breaks it: a 2008-style opening (−22%, −15%) lifts the shortfall probability from 20% to **81%**… it is the risk that the fixed-6.5% sheet cannot show you at all." Also "Averages are not outcomes."

assertions.text: The response identifies that the £42,000 annual spending is never increased for inflation anywhere in the model.
assertions.evidence: "The dominant error is that spending never rises with inflation. You grow the pot at 6.5% — a nominal rate — while holding spending flat at £42,000 for 26 years. The £42,000 you spend in 2051 buys what £22,700 buys today."

assertions.text: The response states that the State Pension start age of 66 used in the model is incorrect or unverified for at least one of the two partners.
assertions.evidence: "State Pension age is **67, not 66**, for both of you: ... Alex reaches it in **May 2033**, Sam in **September 2035**. The sheet has both a year early." Also assumptions A9: "State Pension age | 66 | 67 (May 2033 / Sept 2035)".

assertions.text: The response flags the £203.85 weekly State Pension figure as out of date or as needing a current-year source.
assertions.evidence: "two stale State Pension facts — £203.85/week is the **2023/24** rate (it's now £241.30, so £12,548 not £10,600)"; facts.md: "The model's £203.85/week is the **2023/24** rate — three uprating rounds stale."

assertions.text: The response identifies that treating withdrawals as gross-of-tax overstates what the pots deliver, because pension drawdown beyond the tax-free portion is taxed as income.
assertions.evidence: "No tax, in a plan built almost entirely of taxable pension money. 'Gross of tax keeps it simple' is where the simplification stops being safe: £685,000 of the £805,000 is pension money, taxable on the way out… median lifetime income tax bill is £102,900." Plus reconciliation line E (£790k→£720k) and "the taxable 75% of the UFPLS".

assertions.text: The response identifies that the order or mix of withdrawals across the pensions, ISAs, and cash changes the tax owed.
assertions.evidence: Decision rule 2: "(b) UFPLS from each pension up to the point where the taxable 75% exactly fills that person's remaining personal allowance — this is tax-free money and it is the single largest lever you have. (c) ISA and cash for anything further. (d) Only then, taxed pension withdrawals. Draw from *both* pensions... two personal allowances are worth about £25,000 a year of tax-free income".

assertions.text: The response states that the planner's 100% success rate depends on its automatic spending cuts, so it does not demonstrate that £42,000 of spending is sustainable.
assertions.evidence: "The planner's 100% isn't a second opinion. Its own note says spending is cut by up to 25% in poor markets — a plan that cuts instead of running out can't run out." Plan adds: "Success is 100% because failure has been defined out of existence."

assertions.text: The response states what annual spending could fall to in the planner's poor scenarios, or identifies that the planner summary omits how low spending goes and for how long.
assertions.evidence: FINANCIAL_PLAN.md "The floor": "a median of **27 years out of 40 spent below £42,000**, lifetime average spending of £37,300 at the median and **£32,690 at the 10th percentile**, and a worst year of **£31,500**." Quantifies both how low and for how long.

assertions.text: The response gives an explicit overall answer on whether the couple can afford to retire this year.
assertions.evidence: Headline: "**£42,000 a year from this year is a near-miss, not a comfortable yes.**" and in the response: "**Can you afford £42,000?** Not with the confidence the sheet implies, but it's close… The sustainable figure is **£39,400** — you're about £2,600/yr short."
